title: Build vs. Buy: Gauge AEO
summary: Compare the cost of building your own AEO stack with Gauge, from answer collection and normalization to agentic analysis and publishing. Build your custom workflows on the foundation we already provide.
body_markdown:
## Key takeaways


Building your own AEO product is:


- **More expensive:** Your Claude API collection alone can cost roughly 3× Gauge Growth, before you pay for engineering and infrastructure.
- **Less accurate when built on APIs:** Your API responses do not reproduce what customers see in consumer chat interfaces.
- **More work:** Your team must build and maintain citation extraction, brand and sentiment judging, source scraping, and storage.
- **Harder to use:** Your team must build dashboards and agent retrieval tools before it can easily investigate the data.
- **Less effective without an execution workflow:** Your answer collector still leaves your team to turn findings into content, publish it, and measure results.


**Build your custom workflows on Gauge instead.** Use MCP, CLI, and API access to work from the data, analysis tools, and publishing integrations Gauge already provides.


## Build your own vs. Gauge

The cost example compares Claude API usage at ~$3 per prompt per month with Growth at its full 600-prompt capacity. Growth includes ChatGPT, Google AI Mode, and Microsoft Copilot; Claude BYOK is extra and uses API collection. These are different engines and collection methods, not an identical-workload benchmark. Feature availability depends on your plan.


## More expensive: API collection alone can cost 3× Gauge


Gauge offers Claude tracking as a bring-your-own-key addition. The provider bills your account for those calls, typically **$2.50–$3 per tracked prompt per month** . See our[BYOK documentation](https://docs.withgauge.com/help/byok) for the estimate and availability.


[Gauge Growth](https://www.withgauge.com/pricing) costs $599 per month for 600 prompts tracked daily across ChatGPT, Google AI Mode, and Microsoft Copilot. At full capacity, that is about **$1 per tracked prompt per month across all three included platforms** , including Growth's analysis and content features.


For 600 prompts, Claude API usage at $3 per prompt costs approximately **$1,800 per month** . That is roughly **3× the entire $599 Growth subscription** , just to collect answers from one additional engine.


This comparison uses Growth's full prompt allowance and the upper end of our typical Claude estimate. Costs vary by engine and workload; Claude BYOK usage is additional to the subscription.


A custom build adds extraction and judging calls, citation-page collection, storage, engineering, and maintenance. The API bill is the starting point for your budget.


## Less accurate: API answers do not show what chat users see


The model is only part of an answer. The software around it, often called the harness, controls instructions, search behavior, tools, context, and presentation. Calling a model through an API does not reproduce that environment. This is why the distinction between a product like ChatGPT and a coding agent like Codex matters: the harness changes the work the model does.


Gauge's core collection approach goes to the consumer interface in a logged-out session, asks the question, and records the result. Our[ChatGPT tracking measures the default logged-out experience with web search enabled](https://docs.withgauge.com/navigating/ai-engines) . We capture the product's behavior, including its harness.


Answers still vary between runs, and logged-in users may have different settings or personalization. Claude BYOK is an API-based exception. But for consumer-interface tracking, Gauge samples the actual surface your customers use.


If you build around API responses, you cannot assume you are measuring what customers see when they research your category. Reproducing the relevant experience requires collecting from those product surfaces and maintaining those collectors as the products change.


## More work: every answer needs extraction, normalization, and enrichment


Gauge turns answers into a consistent schema across platforms. We extract citations, use an LLM judge to identify brand mentions, and use an LLM judge to assess sentiment for the brands mentioned. We store and aggregate those records across prompts, topics, competitors, platforms, and dates.


We also scrape cited URLs to collect their content. That lets you investigate what a cited page says and compare it with your own content, rather than stopping at a list of links.


Building this yourself means maintaining the entire pipeline: raw answers, source URLs, brand identification, sentiment judgments, cited-page content, and comparable metrics over time. Each platform's output has to fit the same schema for cross-platform analysis to be useful.


## Harder to use: your agent needs tools to query all that data


Gauge provides dashboards and analysis views, but[Ask Gauge](https://www.withgauge.com/features/ask-gauge) is the core difference. It has tools to retrieve the right data, investigate a question, and interpret the results.


For example:


> For our observability prompts over the last 30 days, which sources did ChatGPT cite when it recommended our main competitor? Compare those pages with ours, check keyword volumes, and recommend what to work on first.


That requires identifying prompts, filtering answers, finding competitor mentions, retrieving citations, examining source content, and looking up keyword data. Ask Gauge can access prompts, answers, sentiment, and citations, slice them by competitor, topic, and date range, and use DataForSEO tools for keyword volume.


A custom agent needs all those retrieval tools. It needs precise ways to request relevant records, aggregate them, and return evidence you can inspect.


Gauge's system prompts also draw on our experience across hundreds of customers, including developer tools. They guide the agent through research, interpretation, and content work. Rebuilding the tools and task-specific guidance is a much larger job than connecting an LLM to a database.


With Gauge, you can ask the question and have the agent do that work.


## Less effective: collecting answers does not get improvements published


A visibility report still leaves your team with the writing, editing, publishing, and follow-up.


Gauge carries the analysis into content. It can create briefs, write articles, update existing pages, and publish through[integrations with Webflow, Framer, GitHub, and Sanity](https://docs.withgauge.com/help/cms-integrations) . GitHub changes become pull requests; CMS destinations follow their supported publishing options and deployment setup.


Once content is published, you can track subsequent answers and citations, assess changes in visibility, and iterate. The same data that identifies an opportunity helps you evaluate what happens after you act on it.


You can build CMS integrations yourself, but content retrieval, field mapping, editing, review, publishing, and measurement all become additional engineering work. Until those pieces exist, your internal tool leaves more of the actual AEO work to your team.


## Build on Gauge with Claude Code, MCP, CLI, and API access


Gauge makes its data available through MCP, CLI, and API interfaces. You can use Ask Gauge in the product or work from the agent you already prefer.


Connect the[Gauge MCP](https://www.withgauge.com/mcp) to Claude Code and use your visibility data alongside your repository, internal research, and company context. Your agent can investigate a visibility gap, compare cited pages with documentation in your repository, and prepare an update for review. You spend engineering time on workflows specific to your business while Gauge handles the data foundation.


A small API experiment can be useful when API behavior is what you want to measure. Rebuilding a recurring AEO program requires the full collection, analysis, and execution stack described above.


**Buy the foundation. Build what is specific to your business.** Gauge gives you the data, analysis tools, and publishing connections so you can start improving visibility immediately.[Explore Gauge AEO](https://www.withgauge.com/geo) or[connect your agent through MCP](https://www.withgauge.com/mcp) .


The same MCP and CLI interfaces also connect to Gauge Agents, bringing research into how coding agents discover, choose, and use your product into the same workflow.


## Frequently asked questions


### Is building an AEO tool cheaper than buying Gauge?


Answer collection alone can cost more. At approximately $3 per prompt per month, tracking 600 prompts through the Claude API costs about $1,800 monthly. Gauge Growth costs $599 for 600 prompts across its three included platforms, plus analysis and content features. The engines differ, but the example shows why API usage, engineering, and maintenance all belong in your budget.


### Can I use model APIs to measure what customers see in ChatGPT?


API responses do not reproduce ChatGPT's consumer interface, search behavior, or surrounding instructions. Gauge measures the default logged-out ChatGPT experience with web search enabled. Results still vary between runs and may differ from a personalized, logged-in session.


### What would I need to build beyond answer collection?


You need citation extraction, brand identification, sentiment judging, source-page scraping, storage, and aggregations. Then come dashboards, agent retrieval tools, content workflows, and CMS integrations. Each part needs ongoing maintenance.


### Can I use Gauge from Claude Code instead of the Gauge app?


Yes. We recommend using coding agents with Gauge for power users who want to get the most out of the platform. Connect the[Gauge MCP](https://www.withgauge.com/mcp) to Claude Code to work with Gauge data alongside your repository and company context. CLI and API access also let you build custom workflows on the existing foundation.


### Can Gauge publish the content it recommends?


Yes. Gauge can turn analysis into briefs, articles, and updates to existing pages, then send that content to Webflow, Framer, GitHub, or Sanity. GitHub changes become pull requests; CMS publishing follows the destination's supported options. You can then track subsequent answers and citations to evaluate changes.
